classification.tone: Grounded, anxious, darkly playful, and increasingly surreal

evaluation.positioning_hook: A Queens college student who can rewind time after a bus shooting becomes the NYPD detective’s only lead when the city starts forgetting murders — and the killer knows his name.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean commercial engine: a young man with a time-bending curse, a detective chasing a vanishing murder trail, and a city-scale mystery that keeps widening. It plays to thriller audiences, supernatural genre fans, and viewers who like crime stories with a high-concept twist.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early in the bus cold open and then sharpens through the missing evidence, the clock-eye tattoo, and Anthony’s rooftop confession. The story engine is easy to explain in two sentences and the rules of the mystery are legible fast.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Anthony has a strong internal contradiction — model student, people-pleaser, and accidental time-bender with a panic-stricken conscience — while Ji-a brings hard-edged competence and dry authority. Joan adds warmth and bite, though the script is still centering the lead pair more than a fully spread ensemble.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The time-loop idea is familiar territory, but the specific collision of NYPD procedural, college-campus intimacy, and a killer who can erase the trail gives it its own shape. The old woman with the Uzi and the clock-eye tattoo are memorable, off-kilter choices that signal a writer with a distinct genre instinct.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening moves with real propulsion: murder, investigation, memory loss, then the reveal that Anthony is the center of the case. The rooftop confrontation gives the pilot a strong turn, though the middle section is still doing a lot of setup work before the full engine locks in.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script has the satisfying 'of course this exists' quality in its core idea: a frightened college kid becomes a repeatable crime scene and a detective starts losing the case around him. The clock motif, erased evidence, and time-shuttered violence make the concept feel more specific than a standard supernatural mystery.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Queens, the NYPD, college life, and the bus system all give the story a recognizable urban texture, and the Q-bus detail helps the world feel lived-in. The world is still mostly serving the central mystery rather than generating a larger social ecosystem on its own.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct blend of deadpan humor, panic, and supernatural unease, especially in the bus cold open and the banter between Anthony and Joan. Ji-a’s clipped detective voice and the absurdity of the old woman’s Uzi give the piece a flavor that feels specific rather than generic.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the murder mystery, there are seeds of identity pressure, guilt, faith, and self-erasure, especially in Anthony’s fear that he may be a monster and Ji-a’s growing sense that reality is slipping. The script suggests more beneath the surface than it immediately explains, which is a strong sign for a feature-length expansion.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Anthony/Joan and Ji-a/Larry each have workable chemistry, and the Anthony/Ji-a collision is the real engine of the piece. The supporting relationships are functional and entertaining, but the script is still primarily powered by the lead mystery rather than a web of equally generative dynamics.

technical.vfx_details: Time-shutter effects, repeated moments, disappearing evidence, and visual resets around death/reversal beats.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, blood hits, body wounds, practical death/reset beats, and a rooftop fall.

rights_flags.detail: Q bus system, Amazon Warehouse, Glock, Uzi, and Cheetos-style street food references are present in dialogue and action.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong festival-to-platform or direct-streaming potential

cost.note: Contemporary urban locations keep the footprint manageable, while time-reset visuals and night exteriors add some effects and coverage needs.

cast.note: The script is built around a compact adult cast with three clear leads and no child-actor requirement.

location.note: The story moves through bus, precinct, campus, dorm, rooftop, and street settings, but all are contemporary and producible.

content.note: Gun violence, murder, panic attacks, profanity, and corpse imagery push it into mature territory without becoming extreme.

rights.note: There are a few brand and transit references, but no major life-rights or music dependencies.

whats_special.headline: This script has a clean, sellable genre engine: a frightened college student becomes the center of a murder investigation that keeps erasing itself, while a detective starts to realize reality is bending around him. The combination of procedural momentum, time-bending spectacle, and sharp character banter gives it both a commercial hook and a distinct voice.

lead_characters.name: ANTHONY MORGAN
lead_characters.hook: Anthony is a high-achieving, people-pleasing student whose nervous interior life suddenly becomes the center of a supernatural crime story. He reads as anxious, decent, and deeply over his head, with a voice that can pivot from self-protective humor to full-body panic in a beat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network — a fast-talking, hyper-aware lead whose inner panic is always visible under the surface. It gives a young actor the chance to play fear, wit, guilt, and escalating moral collapse while still carrying a high-concept thriller.

lead_characters.name: DETECTIVE JI-A CHOI
lead_characters.hook: Ji-a is a hard-edged NYPD detective with a dry, impatient voice and a mind that moves faster than the people around her. She is the kind of investigator who treats nonsense like a solvable system, and the script lets her authority, irritation, and intuition all play at once.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Carrie Coon in The Leftovers — a smart, emotionally contained woman whose certainty becomes the audience’s way into the impossible. It gives a dramatic lead the chance to play procedural command, skepticism, and dawning wonder without losing control of the frame.

lead_characters.name: JOAN
lead_characters.hook: Joan is Anthony’s closest friend: sharp-tongued, funny, emotionally direct, and far more perceptive than she pretends to be. She brings the script its social oxygen, but she also carries a real loyalty that makes her more than comic relief.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Ayo Edebiri in The Bear — a quick, funny, emotionally legible presence who can land jokes and then pivot into real feeling. It gives a young actress a role with chemistry, timing, and enough emotional specificity to become a breakout favorite.

lead_characters.name: XII / VITO
lead_characters.demographics: Female · 30s-40s · unspecified ethnicity with New York streetwise energy
lead_characters.hook: XII is the script’s most volatile presence: a time-bending killer with a casual, almost amused relationship to violence and reality. She’s playful, predatory, and weirdly charismatic, which makes every scene with her feel unstable in the best way.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing territory Jodie Comer had in Killing Eve — a character who can be funny, dangerous, and impossible to read in the same breath. It gives a performer a chance to dominate limited screen time with style, menace, and a signature voice.

lead_characters.name: LARRY
lead_characters.hook: Larry is the awkward, earnest partner who keeps trying to be useful while Ji-a steamrolls him. He functions as comic friction and procedural support, with enough personality to make the precinct feel inhabited.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of side-part that Paul Rudd made memorable in Anchorman — a straight-man role that gets laughs through timing and exasperation. Character actors and comedic performers will see an easy, scene-friendly lane here.

lead_characters.name: JOAN'S EX / EMMA
lead_characters.hook: Emma is more presence than personality in the pages we see, but she functions as a charged emotional marker in Joan’s orbit and Anthony’s unraveling. The role sits at the intersection of intimacy and dread, which gives it a haunting utility in the story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but memorable dramatic space that actors in Her or Euphoria-style material chase — a role where stillness and implication do the work. It offers a performer the chance to leave a mark through atmosphere and emotional residue.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a grounded genre feature with a clean supernatural rule set and real emotional bite.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors with a strong short-film or indie-thriller background, especially those who like performance-forward suspense over spectacle. The material rewards precise blocking, tonal control, and visual storytelling around repetition, memory, and dread.
director_appeal.detail: The time-reset beats, rooftop confrontation, and bus cold open give a director room to build tension through rhythm rather than scale. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who can make a contained urban world feel cinematic and who want a calling-card feature that proves they can handle both character and concept.

buyer_appeal.detail: The cast is compact and the story can be mounted without name-talent, which helps a buyer package it off a strong script, director, and one breakout lead. The supernatural crime hook and contemporary New York setting fit the current streamer appetite for contained genre features with a clear hook and exportable premise.

considerations.area: Anthony’s inner conflict can be foregrounded sooner.
considerations.detail: The rooftop confession and the bus panic already give him a strong emotional center; a next pass could let one earlier scene make his guilt or self-doubt more visible before the mystery fully takes over. That would make the eventual reveal feel even more personal and less purely procedural.

considerations.area: Ji-a’s personal stake can be sharpened.
considerations.detail: Her detective drive is clear, and the erased-case material is compelling, but the script would benefit from one more on-page choice that makes this case feel like it touches her beyond professional pride. The version where her certainty costs her something specific would deepen the emotional engine without changing the plot shape.

considerations.area: The middle section carries a lot of setup.
considerations.detail: The bus case, precinct work, campus search, and evidence-loss sequence all do useful work, but the movie will move even more cleanly if one of those investigative beats is folded into another. A simplification pass here would protect momentum while keeping the same mystery information on screen.

considerations.area: The time rules can be stated through action even more.
considerations.detail: The clock-eye tattoo and the repeated rooftop moment are strong visual anchors; one direction would be to keep leaning on those kinds of physical cues instead of any explanatory dialogue that might slow the reveal. The more the audience learns the rules by watching them happen, the more elegant the concept feels.

considerations.area: The supporting web is compact by design.
considerations.detail: That compactness is a production advantage, and it also means the script can stay focused on the Anthony-Ji-a collision without needing to widen the cast. If the goal is a lean feature package, this footprint already supports it.
